p.title: Efficient Influence Maximization in Social-Networks Under Independent Cascade Model

ext.title: Efficient Influence Maximization in Social-Networks Under Independent Cascade Model
ext.venue: Procedia Computer Science 173 (2020) 315-324, ICITETM2020 (International Conference on Smart Sustainable Intelligent Computing and Applications). Metadata hint verified against the PDF header and first page.
ext.document_type: Conference paper (open access, CC BY-NC-ND), 10 pages incl. references
ext.coverage: Full text read in one pass (text file lines 1-475: front matter, abstract, Sections 1-5, all 22 references). Coverage of the topics the brief names: influence maximization and seed selection (full), independent cascade and threshold models (full), greedy/CELF/centrality methods (full), networks and path-finding (Chen et al. maximum-influence-path mention, p.318; no original path-finding contribution). Lobbying, elections, persuasion/turnout, legislators, allocation under budget, and text measurement: NOT present in the paper. The abstract mentions selecting k users at minimum cost, and p.318 says the problem can be generalized to cost, but no cost model is built or tested.
ext.research_question: Given a social network and a diffusion model, which k seed nodes maximize expected spread under the Independent Cascade Model (ICM) while keeping computation cheap? Two sub-questions: (a) can a degree-based heuristic (DHICM) approach greedy/CELF spread at much lower cost; (b) can ICM edge probabilities be derived from network structure (degrees, common neighbours) instead of a fixed constant, to make spread more realistic (MICM).
ext.theory: Independent Cascade and Linear Threshold diffusion models (Kempe et al. 2003, ref [12]); word-of-mouth and viral-marketing theory (Goldenberg et al. 2001, refs [6][7] as cited; Granovetter 1978 for thresholds); submodularity of the spread function, which gives the greedy (1-1/e, text says 63%) guarantee (p.318); degree-discount heuristic (Chen et al. 2009, ref [4]); the claim that centrality heuristics are fast and that similarity (degree and common neighbours) can proxy real propagation probability (p.320-321).
ext.data: Two academic co-authorship networks, labelled NetHept and NetPhy, with the authors citing ref [20] (Wang, Chen, Wang 2012) for the source. Unit: author = node; edge = two authors who co-wrote a paper. Both are undirected multigraphs that the authors simplify to undirected simple graphs (p.322). Table 4.1 (p.322): NetHept n = 15,233 nodes, m = 58,891 edges; NetPhy n = 37,154 nodes, m = 231,584 edges. Abstract says the academic collaboration data is from arXiv.org; the text does not name the arXiv subject categories. Time period: not stated. Hardware: 2.10 GHz Xeon, 6 cores / 12 logical processors, 16 GB RAM (p.321). No real diffusion or outcome data is used; all results are simulated spread on the networks.
ext.method: Algorithmic benchmark with Monte Carlo simulation of ICM. (1) DHICM (Algorithm 3, p.320): compute degrees, then repeatedly pick the max-discounted-degree node and update each un-seeded neighbour v as dd_v = d_v - 1 - (d_u - 1)p (Eq. 3.2), where p is the ICM propagation probability. Stated complexity O(n + k log n + m). (2) MICM (Eq. 3.3, p.320): edge probability p_ij = 0.01 + (d_i + d_j)/n + CN(i,j)/n, with n the node count and CN the common-neighbour count (the extracted equation is typeset ambiguously; this is the reading the surrounding prose gives). Spread is estimated by R Monte Carlo runs per candidate (Algorithm 2, p.319); the value of R used in experiments is NOT reported. Baselines: CELF (Leskovec et al. 2007, ref [13]), degree centrality, Katz centrality, PrKatz (ref [1] as cited), and Random. k is varied (values shown in figures for k = 10 to 80). Baseline ICM uses p = 0.01 (Fig. 4.1 caption, p.322).
ext.identification: None. The paper makes no causal claim; it is a comparative simulation benchmark. The "modified ICM" is an assumed functional form for edge probability, justified by prose (similarity, real-world dynamics), not estimated from data or validated against observed diffusion.
ext.scope: Population: two academic co-authorship networks (no social media or political networks). Institution: National Institute of Technology Delhi (authors); conference ICITETM2020. Era: not stated. Generalization is limited to ICM with the two networks tested; the authors themselves say performance on other cascade models is untested (p.324).

key_findings.finding: DHICM spread on NetHept is close to CELF: 12.5% lower at k=10 and 7.9% lower at k=30.
DHICM beats degree centrality on NetHept for every k tested.
On NetPhy, DHICM beats degree centrality at k=50 and trails CELF slightly at k=30.
key_findings.numbers: k=50: +10% vs degree; k=30: -2.5% vs CELF

key_findings.finding: PrKatz (Katz-based, ref [1]) underperforms: on NetHept it is worse than Random for some k; on NetPhy it beats Random throughout. Authors attribute this to graph pre-processing that splits the graph into components and to Katz centrality being weaker than degree in their results.
key_findings.numbers: not reported as a table value; qualitative

key_findings.finding: Running time: CELF takes very large time on both datasets; DHICM takes a few seconds more than plain degree and Katz centrality.
key_findings.numbers: times shown only in figures; no numeric table

key_findings.finding: Modified ICM (MICM) raises spread for every algorithm on NetHept. Katz +5.7% at k=30; Degree +8.92% at k=70; DHICM +6.8% at k=40; CELF +12.5% at k=70.
On NetPhy under MICM, gains are much larger: Katz +31.29% (k=20); Degree +32.60% (k=20); DHICM +23.7% (k=30); CELF +55.55% (k=10).

MICM raises run time: DHICM +12.6% (NetHept) and +8.6% (NetPhy); CELF +9.4% and +6.5%; degree and Katz no significant change. Authors attribute the increase to larger spread, not to a complexity change.
Stated complexity: DHICM O(n + k log n + m) vs greedy O(knRm) (R = Monte Carlo runs). Conclusion restates CELF as O(nkRm); the two complexity statements are not identical.
Authors' main conclusion: centrality heuristics should be improved rather than making greedy faster, and edge probabilities should be derived from node or network information.

measures: Expected spread Gamma(S): number of active nodes at end of ICM cascade from seed set S, estimated by Monte Carlo (p.317-318)
Marginal influence Minf(u) = |Gamma(S u {u}) - Gamma(S)| (Eq 2.1, p.318)
Degree centrality d_v; degree-discount dd_v (Eq 3.1-3.2, p.319-320)
Katz centrality (ref [22]) and PrKatz pre-processed Katz (ref [1])
Edge propagation probability p_ij from degrees and common neighbours (Eq 3.3)
Percentage gain of MICM over ICM for each algorithm (Sec 4.2)
limitations: Only ICM tested; authors state DHICM performance must be tested on other cascade models (p.324).
Only two co-authorship networks; no node attributes used by design (p.320: only topology assumed known). Generalization to other network types is untested.
MC sample size R used in experiments is not reported; no error bars, confidence intervals, or repeated-seed runs in the text, so the reported percentage differences cannot be checked for noise.
Baseline ICM uses p = 0.01 for all edges, which the authors themselves call unrealistically low (p.321); MICM gains are measured against this weak baseline.

MICM edge probability (Eq 3.3) is an ad hoc functional form with no empirical validation against real diffusion data; the claim that it reflects real-world dynamics (p.321, p.323) is asserted, not tested. The 0.01 constant and normalisation by n are chosen by the authors.
Gains from MICM are reported as percent increases in spread without showing that the ranking of algorithms is unchanged; some MICM rankings (e.g. CELF vs DHICM) are not discussed.
Network simplification: multigraphs turned into simple graphs (p.322), so repeated co-authorship weights are discarded.
Complexity claims are inconsistent: O(knRm) (p.320) vs O(nkRm) for CELF (p.323); and the stated DHICM complexity is not validated by any timing scaling experiment.
PrKatz is re-implemented by the authors, and they state their results show it underperforms; no details are given on the re-implementation.

Citation numbering in the text does not match the reference list: text cites [2] for Goldenberg et al. (list [2] is Arora et al.) and [17] for Kempe et al. (list [17] is Richardson and Domingos). Read the reference list with care.
Abstract says DHICM spread is 'close to benchmark greedy', but this is shown only on two networks and only with the greedy approximated by CELF.
references_of_note: Kempe, Kleinberg, Tardos 2003, 'Maximizing the spread of influence through a social network' (ref [12]): defines ICM and LTM, proves NP-hardness and submodularity, greedy (1-1/e, text says 63%) guarantee.
Chen, Wang, Yang 2009, 'Efficient influence maximization in social networks' (ref [4]): degree-discount heuristic that DHICM extends.
Leskovec et al. 2007, 'Cost-effective outbreak detection in networks' (ref [13]): CELF lazy-forward greedy; the paper's main speed benchmark.
Goyal, Lu, Lakshmanan 2011, CELF++ (ref [8]) and SIMPATH under LTM (ref [9]): faster greedy variants.

Wang, Chen, Wang 2012, 'Scalable influence maximization for independent cascade model in large-scale social networks' (ref [20]): source of the two datasets and the maximum-influence-path Dijkstra method.
Alshahrani et al. 2018, 'Top-k influential users selection based on combined Katz centrality and propagation probability' (ref [1]): PrKatz, the Katz-based baseline the paper finds weak.
Zhan et al. 2017, 'Identification of top-k nodes in large networks using Katz centrality' (ref [22]): Katz centrality method.
Richardson and Domingos 2002, 'Mining knowledge-sharing sites for viral marketing' (ref [17] in list): early network-based influence model for marketing; text cites it under the Kempe label.
Arora, Galhotra, Ranu 2017, 'Debunking the myths of influence maximization' (ref [2] in list): benchmarking study the paper cites for the cascade/threshold background.
Newman 2010, 'Networks: an introduction' (ref [15]) and Wasserman and Faust 1994 (ref [21]): network-science and centrality background.

short_quotes.quote: degree heuristic algorithm is very efficient and has influence spread far better than many centrality based heuristics
we need to work in the direction of improving centrality based heuristics, since they are very fast
The proposed DHICM algorithm works well for ICM while its performance needs to be tested on other cascade models.

rel.summary_md:
Trivedi and Singh (2020) is a short algorithm benchmark under the Independent Cascade Model (ICM). It makes two proposals. The first, DHICM, extends Chen et al.'s 2009 degree-discount rule: once a node is picked as a seed, each neighbour's degree is discounted by dd_v = d_v - 1 - (d_u - 1)p. The second, MICM, replaces the constant edge probability (p = 0.01) with a structural form: 0.01 + (d_i + d_j)/n + common neighbours/n. Both are tested on two arXiv co-authorship graphs (NetHept: 15,233 nodes and 58,891 edges; NetPhy: 37,154 nodes and 231,584 edges). The data contain no real diffusion or outcomes, and the paper does not report how many Monte Carlo runs it used or give error bars. On NetHept, DHICM's spread is 12.5% below CELF at k=10 and 7.9% below at k=30. It beats plain degree centrality by 10 to 16% and runs in seconds where CELF takes far longer. A Katz-based heuristic does worse than degree and sometimes worse than random. MICM raises spread for every algorithm (CELF by up to +55.6% on NetPhy at k=10). That rise mostly follows mechanically from leaving a deliberately low 0.01 baseline, and the paper offers no evidence that MICM is realistic.

For Paul's system the paper matters mainly as a calibration of trade-offs. With 533 members and a stance-gated shortlist of 45, CELF's cost does not constrain the budget frontier, so the paper's 8 to 12% spread penalty argues for keeping the exact lazy greedy over a degree heuristic. The dashboard's budget-recruit mode is already a probabilistic one-hop degree-discount, which is the DHICM family. The per-topic coalition allocator scores each candidate's marginal in isolation and ignores seed overlap, which is the problem degree-discount exists to fix. MICM does not calibrate the kernel: the system draws edge probabilities from weighted cosponsorship with saturation, at much higher p than 0.01. All spread figures here are simulated model outputs on co-authorship graphs, not measured influence.

bearings.paper_claim: Under ICM, the cheap degree-discount heuristic DHICM gives up 12.5% (k=10) and 7.9% (k=30) of CELF's spread on NetHept, and 2.5% at k=30 on NetPhy. CELF's only drawback is run time on networks of 15k to 37k nodes.
bearings.system_side: The frontier runs exact CELF-style lazy greedy (heap of stale marginals, re-evaluated when popped) up to MAXSEEDS=60 over a stance-gated top-45 neutral shortlist plus contest and defend pools. Marginals come from MC=20 competitive-cascade spread with edge-keyed common random numbers.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper's case for heuristics rests on CELF being too slow at 10^4 or more nodes. Here n=533 and the candidate pool is about 45, so cost does not constrain, and the paper's own numbers say a degree heuristic would lose spread. That carries over only as an ordering of algorithms under ICM-type cascades. The size of the gap was measured at p=0.01 on co-authorship graphs, not on the system's higher-p cosponsor kernel, and no MC sample size or variance is reported. This favours keeping lazy greedy. It does not validate the frontier's spread values, which are model outputs.

bearings.paper_claim: Picking seeds by raw degree (each node's stand-alone value) ignores overlap among seeds and trails the overlap-aware degree-discount by 16% at k=30 and 10.4% at k=80 on NetHept (about 10% at k=50 on NetPhy). The discount dd_v = d_v - 1 - (d_u-1)p penalises neighbours of seeds already chosen.
bearings.paper_location: Sec 3.1 Eq 3.2 and Algorithm 3, p.319-320; Sec 4.1, p.321
bearings.system_side: The coalition allocator computes each candidate's marginal in isolation, spread({n}) - base. It boosts that by (1 + 0.8 bpf) and water-fills the topic budget in proportion. No candidate's value is discounted for adjacency to other funded seeds. The honest joint spread is reported afterwards, but it does not feed back into the allocation.
bearings.transfer_conditions: This holds because the allocator funds many seeds at once on a shared cosponsor graph, so neighbouring recruits overlap. Treat the paper's percentage gaps as directional only: they are simulated, k-dependent, and lack error bars. A fix (sequential greedy as in budget_frontier, or a degree-discount pre-pass) is a candidate for owner review, not a measured gain. The per-topic allocators are labelled diagnostic and not summable, which limits the stakes.

bearings.paper_claim: One-hop degree-discount (DHICM) comes close to greedy at low propagation probability (p=0.01). Its discount formula assumes small p, so only one-hop overlap counts. Under the higher, structure-derived MICM probabilities, CELF's gain (+55.55% on NetPhy at k=10) is much larger than DHICM's (+23.7% at k=30), so the approximation weakens.
bearings.system_side: budgetRecruit is a greedy with a probabilistic one-hop discount. A candidate's gain is (1 - cov[c]) + sum over neighbours of p * (1 - cov[v]), so neighbours already covered are discounted, and low-degree nodes are pruned. This is the DHICM / degree-discount family, and it counts only one-hop reach.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The comment's (1-1/e) guarantee holds for the one-hop coverage objective it optimizes, not for multi-hop cascade spread. The paper's evidence supports one-hop discounting only when p is small. The system's kernel edge probabilities reach about 0.52 on the CU graph (sector-networks note), well above the paper's 0.01, where multi-hop spread matters and one-hop coverage understates the reach of well-connected recruits. This is an inference from the paper's MICM contrast, not a test on this graph; it stays UNVERIFIED until reproduced.

bearings.paper_claim: Deriving ICM edge probabilities from structure (p_ij = 0.01 + (d_i+d_j)/n + CN(i,j)/n) raises spread for every algorithm (e.g. Degree +32.6%, CELF +55.55% on NetPhy). The functional form is asserted to reflect real dynamics but is never fitted to or validated against observed diffusion.
bearings.system_side: The kernel sets p(u->v) = x/(x+6), with x = cosponsor weight x cpf_diffusion x receiver edge_mult. The saturation constant 6 is a design choice and is not estimated.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper offers an alternative ad hoc form, not a calibration. Its spread gains are mechanical (higher p gives more activation against a 0.01 baseline the authors themselves call unrealistically low), so they cannot justify replacing or tuning the kernel's constant. The common-neighbour term points to one structural signal (triadic closure) the kernel ignores. Any use would need a test against observed cosponsorship join timing, the kernel's own open question. The degree term raises probability for hubs, which is the opposite of the REJECTED per-edge volume normalization; do not present it as that proposal.

bearings.paper_claim: A Katz-centrality seed heuristic (PrKatz) does worse than plain degree under ICM, and on NetHept falls below Random for some k. The authors partly blame graph pre-processing that splits components.
bearings.system_side: The benchmark computes Katz-Bonacich centrality on the live kernel P (delta = 0.85/lambda_max) and Spearman-correlates it with the optimizer allocation and observed money, as a diagnostic of the Battaglini-Patacchini equilibrium. Nothing in the chain consumes it.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper concerns Katz as a seed-selection proxy for cascade spread, and finds it weak. The system uses KB only as an equilibrium-pricing benchmark, not for targeting, so the evidence should only discourage promoting KB rank into seed choice. The paper's PrKatz is a re-implementation with few details, on co-authorship graphs. KB values are heuristic model outputs, never access or closeness probabilities (D-025).

bearings.paper_claim: Raw degree centrality is a weaker seed-value proxy than overlap-aware degree-discount (by 10 to 16% on NetHept) and than greedy, and Katz is weaker still.
bearings.system_side: InfluenceScore (0.60 weighted out-degree + 0.25 betweenness + 0.15 eigenvector) was retired from the Influence pillar on 2026-06-25 (AB13 = 0) as direction-blind, and survives only in the underdog lens.
bearings.code_ref: congress_centrality_*.xlsx; Blended Model AB12/AB13 (workbook, no Python line)
bearings.transfer_conditions: This is indirect. The paper measures simulated cascade spread, not legislative influence or bill passage. It agrees with the retirement only in showing that static centrality is a poor stand-in for a member's simulated cascade value. It is no evidence about the underdog lens or about influence on outcomes.

gaps_exposed: per_topic_coalition allocates on isolated single-seed marginals spread({n})-base and never discounts candidates adjacent to other funded seeds. The paper's central mechanism (degree discount for seed overlap) is absent there, though budget_frontier's sequential lazy greedy does handle overlap.

The edge probabilities in the cascade kernel use no structural term such as common neighbours or triadic closure. The paper's MICM is unvalidated, but it names a candidate covariate for any future calibration of the saturation constant 6 against observed cosponsorship join timing.

No check of the dashboard's one-hop coverage heuristic (budgetRecruit) against full multi-hop cascade spread at the kernel's actual p regime (up to about 0.52). The paper implies one-hop discounting degrades as p rises.
The paper reports no Monte Carlo sample size or variance, so it cannot speak to whether MC=20 is adequate. That question still rests on mc_stability_check.py (motivated by Almazaydeh 2026).
flags: Wording: the paper uses 'influence' for simulated ICM spread on co-authorship graphs. When citing it, call spread, degree and Katz ranks heuristic model outputs, never closeness, access or introduction probabilities (D-025).

MICM's degree term raises edge probability for high-degree pairs. It is NOT the REJECTED per-edge volume normalization and must not be presented as support for it. Neither the paper nor this note recommends volume normalization.

The paper turns multigraphs into simple graphs and discards repeated co-authorship weight. Nothing here argues for dropping regular cosponsorship edges or weights (a REJECTED proposal), and none of the paper's results should be read that way.

Every bearing here is new agent analysis. In particular, the claim that the one-hop discount degrades at high p and the overlap critique of per_topic_coalition stay UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces them (DE-062).
Citation hygiene: the paper's in-text reference numbers do not match its reference list (Kempe is cited as [17], Goldenberg as [2]). Use the list entries, not the in-text numbers.
rel.paul_alignment: Paul has not annotated this paper. It agrees with his position on the joint optimizer, where adaptive greedy plus CELF is the operational layer: the paper treats CELF as the accuracy ceiling and offers heuristics only as a speed trade-off that does not bind at 533 members. It partly qualifies his Fink-derived wish for cheap scenario simulation in place of Monte Carlo. Cheap degree heuristics cost 8 to 12% of spread in this benchmark, and the system's CRN Monte Carlo is already affordable at its scale, so the cheap route is not obviously better here. His highlight of Ardekani choosing Katz over PageRank sits uneasily with this paper's finding that Katz is a weak seeding proxy. The two concern different uses (prestige description versus seed selection), so they need not conflict as long as KB stays a diagnostic. Nothing in his notes is made stale by this paper.

related.why: Both argue that centrality heuristics compete with greedy in influence maximization. Almazaydeh adds the MC-noise failure mode of CELF that motivated mc_stability_check.py, which Trivedi does not address (no R reported).
Both rest on the submodularity and (1-1/e) greedy guarantee from Kempe et al. Golovin and Krause extend it to adaptive policies, the bound optimize.py keeps as a diagnostic.
Another IC-model seed-selection benchmark against CELF and centrality baselines, using learned embeddings in place of degree discount.
Chen et al. relax Trivedi's assumption that seeds always activate. The system's seed gate (SGATE x seed_prob) implements that contingency, which the plain DHICM/CELF comparison ignores.
Competitive IC with two cascades is the model the system's competitive-cascade-crn actually runs. Trivedi covers only single-cascade ICM, so his rankings may not transfer to the two-colour race.
A survey of behaviour-aware IM methods that places degree-discount heuristics and edge-probability modelling within the wider literature.
Also targets cheap seed selection, but with an unknown network, whereas Trivedi assumes full topology is known.
